opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the places where people's intuitions can go wrong in both directions.

The naive worry is: AI gets really good at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, so attackers get a huge boost, and we're in trouble. The naive reassurance is: defenders get the same AI, so it all washes out. I don't think either is quite right.

On the defensive side, there's a real case for optimism. A lot of cybersecurity is a numbers game. There's a huge amount of code out there, it's full of bugs, and defenders don't have enough skilled people to find and patch them. If AI can systematically audit codebases, find vulnerabilities, write patches, and monitor networks for anomalous behavior, that addresses exactly the bottleneck defenders face. In principle you could imagine a world where AI helps us harden critical software to a degree that was never feasible with human labor alone. So I don't think it's obvious the offense-defense balance shifts toward offense in the long run.

But a few things make me less comfortable. One is timing. Attackers only need one vulnerability, and they can adopt new capabilities right away. Defenders have to patch, deploy, and coordinate across organizations, many of which run legacy systems, have small security teams, or are slow to update. So even if defense eventually catches up, there could be a window where offense has the edge, and a lot of damage can happen in that window.

Another is that defensive adoption isn't automatic. It depends on whether the companies building these models put real effort into getting defensive tools to the people who need them, whether governments and critical infrastructure operators actually use them, and whether there's coordination around things like disclosing vulnerabilities before capabilities proliferate widely. That's a policy and institutional question as much as a technical one.

And then there's the scenario I worry about most, which isn't really about ordinary cybercrime. It's about very capable AI systems themselves, possibly not under anyone's full control, or a small group with a big capability lead, being able to compromise systems at a scale and speed that ordinary defenses weren't built for. Things like stealing model weights, or an AI system getting out of its intended environment. There, defensive responses matter enormously, but you need them in place before the capability arrives, not after you notice the problem.

So my overall take: I think defense can substantially reduce the risk, maybe a lot, but only if we're proactive about it. If we treat it as something that'll sort itself out because defenders also have AI, I think that's a mistake. The things I'd push for are AI developers investing seriously in their own security, early and prioritized access to defensive capabilities for critical infrastructure, and measuring cyber capabilities in models so we have warning before we hit the dangerous levels rather than finding out from an incident.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shortages of skilled defenders, deployment delays, and legacy systems, but does not say that available defenses go unused because they are inconvenient.

r002.rationale: The response calls for proactive defensive investment and adoption, but does not argue that worsening cyberattacks could prompt adoption of defenses that are already available.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important and most underrated factors in the whole picture. When people think about AI and cyberattacks, they tend to imagine a world where the attacker gets more capable and nothing else changes. And that's just not the world we're going to be in. The same AI that can find vulnerabilities for an attacker can find them for a defender, and the defender often gets to look first — they have the code, they have the access, they can run the models against their own systems before anyone else does.

So the question I find myself asking is less "how scary is the offensive capability?" and more "what's the shape of the offense-defense balance over time, and how fast can defenders actually move?" And I think there's a reasonable story where things go okay. A lot of what makes cyberattacks work today is that software is full of bugs nobody has bothered to find. If you have very capable AI systems that can audit code at scale, you could imagine a world where the low-hanging fruit just goes away. Major software vendors patch things before they're exploited, critical infrastructure gets hardened, and the attacker's advantage shrinks rather than grows.

But I want to be careful not to be too sanguine about that, because there are a few things that worry me. One is the transition period. Even if the long-run equilibrium is favorable to defense, there could be a window where offensive capabilities have diffused and defenses haven't caught up — patching takes time, lots of organizations are slow, and there's a huge amount of legacy software out there that nobody is going to re-audit. Another is that defense is distributed across thousands of institutions with very uneven resources, while an attacker only needs to find one weak spot. A hospital system or a water utility is not going to be running frontier models against its code base next week.

And then there's the point that defensive responses are partly a policy and coordination problem, not just a technical one. Whether defenders actually get access to the most capable models, whether there are good norms around responsible disclosure, whether governments and labs are sharing information — those things determine how much the defensive potential actually gets realized. So I'd say the defensive response is probably the single biggest lever for shrinking this risk, but it's not automatic, and I think there's a lot of work that could be done right now to make sure defenders aren't the ones playing catch-up.

r001.rationale: The response says many organizations are slow and software has undiscovered bugs, but it does not say existing defenses go unused because they are inconvenient.

r002.rationale: It describes possible defensive gains and urges action, but does not argue that worsening cyberattacks could prompt adoption of defensive measures already available.

astra-6.text:
I think the defensive response is a really big part of the picture. It’s not enough to ask, “Could an AI system find vulnerabilities and carry out attacks?” You also have to ask what the world looks like by the time it can do that. Are similarly capable systems finding and fixing vulnerabilities? Are people changing how they secure their most important systems?

You could imagine AI making cyberattacks much more common, but also making defense much better. And you could imagine an initial period where attacks get ahead of defenses and cause a lot of damage before people adapt. Those are very different outcomes, even if the underlying offensive capability is the same.

So I wouldn’t take a demonstration of impressive hacking ability and translate that directly into a conclusion about catastrophic risk. But I also wouldn’t assume that defenses will arrive in time, or that everyone will deploy them. A lot depends on the speed of the transition and whether defenders have time to prepare. That’s the interaction I’d want to understand, rather than looking at offensive capability in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that available cybersecurity defenses go unused because they are inconvenient.

r002.rationale: It says people may adapt and defenses may improve, but does not connect worsening attacks to adoption of defensive measures that are already available.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the defensive response is a really important part of the picture. You can’t just ask, “How good will AI get at finding vulnerabilities and carrying out attacks?” You also have to ask, “How good will it get at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and how quickly will people deploy those defenses?”

One possibility is that attacks get much more effective, people see that happening, and there’s a big investment in security. That could substantially reduce the damage from subsequent attacks. Another possibility is that capabilities advance so quickly that defenders don’t have time to adapt, or that the tools exist but aren’t deployed across all the systems that need them.

So I wouldn’t assume either that defense will take care of the problem or that improvements in offensive capability translate directly into greater risk. A lot depends on the relative pace of improvement and deployment, and on whether the first serious attacks give us an opportunity to respond before something much worse happens.

r001.rationale: The candidate says defenses may not be deployed across all needed systems, but does not state that available defenses go unused because they are inconvenient.

r002.rationale: It says more effective attacks could trigger a big investment in security, but does not specifically say this could prompt adoption of already available defensive measures.
